newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Krasnoyarsk aluminium plant hopes to cut tolling.
newsitem.headline: Krasnoyarsk aluminium plant hopes to cut tolling.

text.p: Krasnoyarsk, the second largest aluminium smelter in Russia and the world, hopes to slash its dependence on tolling deals by the end of 1998, a senior company official said on Tuesday.
"We would hope to end this problem (of tolling) altogether in 1997 or 1998," Oleg Kim, deputy director of Krasnoyarsk's Moscow representation, told Reuters in an interview.

The plant, situated in southern Siberia, depends heavily on tolling deals, whereby trading companies pay the plant to process raw materials but then have the right to sell the finished product on world markets for hard currency.
"Out of production last year of, say, 780,000 tonnes (of primary aluminium), around 450,000 tonnes was produced under tolling deals," Kim said.
"Tolling is nonsense. Everyone understands that very well."
Production under tolling was profitable, but Krasnoyarsk wanted to boost its control over the output process.
"We would love not to have to work under tolling deals, but we have to create the means to continue to produce," Kim said.

Krasnoyarsk was close to signing a $280 million credit deal with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) to invest in modernising the plant, Kin said. Credit Lyonnais of France would manage the credit.
Krasnoyarsk's dependence on tolling is common to Russia's giant aluminium processing plants. Tolling accounts for nearly 70 percent of Russia's primary aluminium output, experts say.

Smelters could not afford to buy raw materials after the 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union and the ensuing economic slump, and so turned to Western commodity powerhouses like London-based Trans-World Group and Swiss-based Glencore AG.
Glencore numbers among Krasnoyarsk's main tolling partners.

Russian aluminium officials are now looking to seize back control of production, although they accept that without tolling, the Russian aluminium industry would have faced collapse during the last five years or so.
As it is, aluminium is one of the few sectors of the Russian economy which has not contracted sharply during the 1990s.

Russia produced 2.87 million tonnes of primary aluminium in 1996, up three percent from 2.79 million in 1995. The Kontsern Alyuminiy producers' group forecasts a two to three percent increase again this year.
Russia exported 2.44 million tonnes outside the Commonwealth of Independent States last year, making it the world's largest exporter of the metal.
